lines: One step downstream quietly slows down, nothing else about the pipeline changes at all.
No error pops up anywhere. No alert fires. The logs stay completely silent about it.
And yet throughput for the whole thing just collapses, right then, every single time.
Getting one step right is one problem, already solved, several times over by now.
Running that step, continuously, for real, at real scale, is a completely different one.
So: what's actually doing the running, underneath all of this?
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
Somebody asks for more parallel work than the cluster actually has room for right now.
Does it run anyway, just a little slower than hoped, or does something simply refuse?
answer: It refuses, flat out, no partial version offered.
What's available to run on is a fixed, countable thing, not a flexible, elastic one.
Ask for more than that count, and there's nowhere left to actually put the extra work.

lines: One piece plans the whole thing out and keeps track of where every part stands.
A separate set of workers actually does the work, each one offering a fixed amount of room.
Add up every worker's room, and that's the hard ceiling on how much can run at once.
Picture several small steps standing right next to each other, each handing off to the next.
Fuse those neighbors into one single piece, and that handoff in between just disappears.
Leave them separate instead, and every single record pays for that same handoff, over and over.
Whoever's receiving hands out a small, limited number of permission slips to whoever's sending.
Run out of slips to hand out, and the sender simply has to stop, with no message exchanged at all.
Stop at one spot, and whoever feeds that spot runs out of room too. It just spreads backward.
Worth reasoning through once more before this reveal settles it.
An older way of running one job on its very own, temporary setup got taken away for good.
What's actually standing in for that now, running a single job's own code on the cluster?
answer: One dedicated setup, but a different shape than before.
A job's own code now runs directly on the cluster itself, not off on the side somewhere.
One cluster, one job, nothing shared with anybody else's work.

lines: That's the one shape this whole thing settled on, once the older option disappeared for good.
A single job's own code runs right there on the cluster, with nothing shared between jobs.
The older, separate-setup way is gone outright. This replaced it, stated plainly, not softened.
The very same engine underneath runs two genuinely different kinds of work.
One kind never ends. The other kind has a clear beginning and a clear end.
For that second kind, how much to run in parallel can be decided from how much data actually showed up.
Every number in this reel came from one real run, happening just now, of this topic's own toy model.
The hard ceiling that really held. The handoff that really disappeared, and the cost that really dropped.
The stall that really spread backward, one step behind the last, and the sizing that really adjusted itself.
So: a planner, a fixed set of workers, and a ceiling nobody can simply ask their way past.
Fuse neighbors together, and a real cost just disappears, with nothing else having to change.
A slowdown that needs no message to spread, one clear shape for a job, one engine for both kinds of work.
